title: Transactions, ACID States & Crash Recovery
subtitle: ACID State Machine, Failure & Rollback, Write-Ahead Logging & ARIES 3-Phase Recovery
mentalModel: A transaction is an all-or-nothing unit of work that moves through Active → Partially Committed → Committed (or Failed → Aborted). The Write-Ahead Log is its flight recorder: commit records reach disk before dirty pages, so after any crash ARIES can replay winners forward and undo losers backwards.

failureModes: Crash during Partially Committed: updates live only in the volatile buffer pool; without a flushed <commit> record ARIES treats the transaction as a loser and rolls it back.
Dirty page flushed before its log record violates WAL and makes crash recovery impossible — committed work could be lost or corrupted.
Cascading rollback risk: if uncommitted data is read by another transaction, aborting the writer forces aborting every reader of the dirty value.

tradeOffs.optionA: No-force (WAL standard): dirty pages stay cached after commit for better throughput; recovery cost shifts to REDO of winners from the log.
tradeOffs.optionB: Force: every commit flushes data pages synchronously for instant recovery but destroys sequential-write performance under load.

tradeOffs.aspect: Eager undo logging (CLRs) vs Steal policy
tradeOffs.optionA: Steal + CLRs: buffers may evict uncommitted pages anytime because Compensation Log Records guarantee losers can always be undone, even across repeated crashes.
tradeOffs.optionB: No-steal: simpler rollback since no uncommitted page ever reaches disk, but long transactions can exhaust the buffer pool.

theoryData.productionScenario: A payments service lost 40 minutes of confirmed orders after an OOM kill because its custom store wrote dirty heap pages before log appends. Enforcing strict WAL (log flush on every commit group) plus ARIES-style restart recovery brought RPO to zero and restart time under 9 seconds for a 12 GB log.

interviewQA.question: Why must the log be written ahead of the data pages (WAL rule)?
interviewQA.answer: Because the log is the only source of truth for recovery. If a dirty page reached disk before its log record and the system crashed, there would be neither the old image nor a redo record — making both UNDO and REDO impossible and breaking Atomicity/Durability.

interviewQA.question: What are the three phases of ARIES and why does REDO repeat history including loser transactions?
interviewQA.answer: ANALYSIS rebuilds the Dirty Page Table and winner/loser sets from the last checkpoint; REDO replays ALL operations after the checkpoint in LSN order to restore the exact crash state; UNDO then rolls back losers using idempotent CLRs. Repeating history is required because partial, non-idempotent page states cannot be undone directly without first restoring the crash-time state.

interviewQA.question: What is the difference between a Dirty Read and a Phantom Read?
interviewQA.answer: A Dirty Read reads uncommitted values of another transaction (violates Isolation and risks cascading aborts); a Phantom Read re-executes a range predicate and sees newly inserted rows committed by another transaction — prevented only by range locks or serializable isolation.

quizData.question: In which transaction state have all statements executed but their effects still live only in the buffer pool?
quizData.explanation: Partially Committed means the final statement finished but updates are not yet durable — the <commit> log record has not been flushed, so a crash would still roll the work back.

quizData.question: According to the Write-Ahead Logging protocol, what must be true before a dirty data page is written to disk?
options: The checkpoint record must be deleted
All log records describing that page's changes must already be flushed
The buffer pool must be empty
quizData.explanation: WAL requires every log record affecting a page (including <commit> for durability) to be on stable storage before the page itself is flushed.

quizData.question: During which ARIES phase are Compensation Log Records (CLRs) written?
quizData.explanation: CLRs are emitted during the UNDO phase while rolling back loser transactions; they make repeated crash recoveries idempotent.
